content.title: "Soft Socializing" Is the Gen Z Trend That's Making Low-Pressure Hangouts the New Normal
content.text: Key Takeaways Soft socializing” prioritizes low-pressure connection. Instead of high-energy outings, it centers around relaxed, activity-based hangouts where conversation flows naturally (or not at all).Gen Z’s preference for authenticity, mental well-being, and flexibility—along with digital connection and post-pandemic habits—has made traditional socializing feel more draining than enjoyable.Simple, low-cost activities like walking, cooking, or working side by side can create meaningful connections without the pressure to perform. You may have come across the term “soft socializing” on your social media feed lately, a Gen Z-driven trend moving away from traditional going-out culture and toward low-pressure ways of spending time together, making connection feel more natural. Ahead, experts break down what soft socializing is, why it’s resonating right now, and how you can take part to build more organic, low-stakes connections. The Gen Z Social Trend That’s Changing How We Hang Out Rather than centering plans around going out, drinking, or high-energy group settings, soft socializing leans into low-pressure, activity-based hangouts where connection can develop more naturally. The activity itself, whether working on a puzzle together, discussing a recent book club read, or attending a pottery session, becomes the focal point, and the expectation to constantly be social is optional. “Shared activities frequently draw attention away from you and onto something external,” says Robert Alexander, PhD, assistant professor of psychology and counseling at New York Institute of Technology. “Pauses in the conversation can come and go without feeling awkward, and you can feel relieved of the responsibility for sustaining the conversation moment-to-moment.” Much of the pressure tied to more traditional ways of gathering comes down to unspoken expectations, including feeling responsible for keeping conversation flowing and responding in engaging ways to avoid awkward silences, particularly in one-on-one or small-group settings. There can also be a sense that you need to be funny, insightful, or entertaining. “Soft socializing shifts the goal from performing to being present. It can help people feel safe, connected with others, and like they truly belong without needing to manage impressions,” Alexander says. “For many people, that can mean the difference between feeling restored by an event and feeling depleted.” Why Alcohol Is Taking a Backseat One defining aspect of this Gen Z trend is the noticeable absence of alcohol. In more traditional nightlife settings, like bars, clubs, or house parties, there are often expectations around drinking or keeping pace with others, staying out late, and matching the group’s energy. For some, that can make it harder to engage in a way that feels comfortable. “Alcohol-focused environments can increase social pressure, particularly for a generation that has been restricted from in-person opportunities to experiment with drinking without having those moments documented and preserved in the virtual space,” says Jordan Ashley, PhD, sociologist and founder and executive director of Souljourn Yoga Foundation. “Consequently, alcohol consumption may encourage a sense of performativity and anxiety rather than facilitating casual conversation and informal socialization.” Why Soft Socializing Is Taking Off Right Now Gen Z is often described as the first generation of true digital natives, coming of age at a time when communication is nearly constant. They’re also among the most frequent users of social media1, which has reshaped how relationships are maintained. “They text and interact in ways that keep relationships active even when not physically present,” says Kent Bausman, PhD, professor of sociology at Maryville University of Saint Louis. “Unlike previous generations, [Gen Z] have rarely experienced social silence. Because connection is continuous for many of them, the more traditional forms of in-person gatherings for socializing feel more like a burden.” That shift marks a contrast with older generations, like Gen X, who relied more heavily on in-person gatherings to maintain relationships, making those interactions feel more formal and, at times, more consequential. “For many Gen Zers, the informational work that occurs through traditional socializing already happens digitally on a regular basis via social media,” Bausman says, noting that in-person socialization often carries less of the same social weight as a result. Ashley points out that delayed socialization also plays a role. Many Gen Zers were in high school during the pandemic, when opportunities to connect were limited to digital platforms or highly controlled, small-group settings. “Experiencing social distancing at such a pivotal stage of development has influenced their current approach to relationships. They’re less drawn to high-pressure social settings and more interested in intentional, comfortable ways to connect.” At the same time, soft socializing can reflect a practical response to economic realities. “Financial constraints, which younger folks traditionally experience regardless of generation, favor the low-cost activities associated with soft socializing because many activities don’t require a whole lot of money, planning, or obligation,” Bausman says. Time scarcity is another factor, as more workers take on multiple roles2 post-COVID, navigate irregular hours, or spend more time working remotely. “Soft socializing affords individuals to drop in and participate at their [own] pace and leave without the social penalties associated with traditional socializing,” Bausman adds. Related Stories The Value Shift Behind Soft Socializing There’s also a broader shift in generational values shaping how Gen Z approaches connection. A recent study suggests that 92% of Gen Z surveyed think that being true to oneself and others was extremely important. “Simply sitting together in a casual setting or engaging in simple activities can feel more real because it’s unpolished and low-pressure,” Bausman says. “For many Gen Z, authenticity means you don’t have to put on a show to demonstrate that you’re present and attentive in the moment.” Another defining value for this generation is a stronger focus on work-life balance and mental well-being. A report from The Annie E. Casey Foundation found that Gen Z is roughly 80% more likely to report a mental health issue compared to previous generations. “The low-pressure social interaction environment that comes with soft socializing orients well with this generation’s desires for greater emotional manageability,” Bausman says. He adds that generational context also plays a role. As the children of Gen X—often described as latchkey kids—and older Millennials, who navigated childhood and adolescence with less adult guidance, many Gen Zers were raised to prioritize authenticity, consider work-life balance, and value flexibility. “In that context, the soft socializing trend feels less like a trend and more like common sense,” Bausman says. How to Make Low-Key Plans Still Feel Meaningful If you’re looking to make new connections or deepen existing ones in a more low-key way but aren’t sure where to begin, there are plenty of approachable entry points. Alexander suggests something as simple as sitting with a friend while each person focuses on their own task, whether that’s reading, studying, or answering emails. “The connection is in the shared presence itself,” he says. You might also try going for a walk or a short hike, or even preparing a meal together. “The task provides structure, and any awkward pauses can be filled by consulting the recipe or doing the next step,” Alexander says. “As a bonus, you have something good to eat at the end of the activity!”
